turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Just a quick heads‑up before we dive in—Yuki and Tom are out today, so they'll be catching up on the notes later.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Got it, thanks for the update.

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: No problem, Daniel.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Alright, moving on then. Since we’re a bit short‑handed, let’s keep the standup tight. Yuki, you were on the query planner rewrite—any quick highlights before we go full speed?

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: Sure thing. I’m still ahead of schedule on the planner, but I hit a surprise with the nested aggregation logic; it’s pulling in an extra join that we didn’t anticipate.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Okay, good to know. Tom, I know you’re not on the call, but can you drop a quick note in the channel about the events table migration status?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Will do—I'll post the latest script logs and flag the maintenance window issue as soon as I’m back.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Sounds good, thanks.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Thanks, team. Let’s keep the momentum, and I’ll sync with support on that maintenance window later today.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: So, the rewrite is still on track—I’m about three days ahead of the original estimate, which puts us at roughly day 12 of a 15‑day sprint.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Nice, that gives us some breathing room. Anything else?

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: Yeah, the nested aggregation piece threw me a curveball.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: When I added support for multi‑level GROUP BY, the planner started injecting an extra join to the events_meta table that we never wrote into the spec.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Extra join? Where does that come from?

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: Turns out the optimizer sees the aggregated field as a foreign key reference, so it tries to pull the dimension row for each bucket. In our case that dimension lives in events_meta, which doubles the row count on the inner loop.

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: Does that affect the cost model?

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: Exactly—cost estimates jumped from 1.2 × 10⁶ to 3.8 × 10⁶ rows scanned, which would push latency past our 200 ms SLA for the analytics endpoint.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Can we prune that join?

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: I’ve added a hint to bypass the metadata lookup when the aggregation key is already resolved upstream, and benchmarked it: we’re back to ~180 ms on the dev cluster, so it’s within target.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Good to hear, Yuki. Let me know if you need any help tweaking the hint syntax.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: Will do. I’ll push the updated planner config to the staging branch by EOD, and we can run the full suite tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Okay, so the events table migration is basically ready on my side—schema changes, index rebuilds, the whole thing—but we hit a snag with the actual data move.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: What's the snag?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: We need a maintenance window to lock the table; otherwise the live writes will clash with the bulk copy, and we could lose rows or get duplicate keys.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Can't we do it online with logical replication?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: We looked into logical replication, but the events table is 12 TB and the replication lag would be huge; plus the current CDC pipeline can't keep up with the write rate of ~8 k writes per second.

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: Do we have any window this week? The support team said the next low‑traffic period is Thursday night around 02:00 UTC.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: That's the only slot I see that wouldn't impact the nightly batch jobs, but I haven't booked it yet because I need confirmation that the ops crew can spin up the extra node for the migration.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: I'll take that on and coordinate with support to lock Thursday 02:00‑04:00 UTC. I'll also make sure the extra node is provisioned.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Great, thanks. I’ll freeze the code and push the migration script to the staging environment tonight so we can do a dry run before the window.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: I get the pain point, but have we fully scoped the risk of a live migration? If we can chunk the copy in 1‑GB batches maybe we avoid a full lock.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Chunking could work, but the event payloads are variable size; we'd still need to pause writes at each chunk boundary to guarantee consistency, which defeats the purpose of staying online.

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: We could spin up a read‑only replica just for the copy, then switch over with a brief cutover. That way the main table stays live while we back‑fill the replica.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: The read‑only replica idea sounds good, but our current CDC pipeline only captures DML, not the massive bulk inserts we need for the initial seed. We'd have to modify the pipeline, which adds overhead we don't have time for this sprint.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: What about using pg_repack? It does an online rebuild and can handle large tables without a full lock, though it does need extra disk space.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: pg_repack was on our radar, but the events table's 12 TB size means we'd need another 12 TB of free space on the same volume, and we’re already at 85 % capacity on the primary storage array.

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: If we can't fit the extra space, maybe we can temporarily offload older partitions to S3, shrink the active set, run pg_repack on the remainder, then bring the partitions back. It adds steps, but keeps us online.

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: Guys, I just got the latest cost report from CloudWatch and we're seeing a spike of about $12,000 this week versus the usual $3,200.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: Whoa, that's huge. Any idea what's driving that?

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: Turns out the backfill job we launched for the new user events schema is running way longer than we modeled. It's been pulling 5 TB of data from S3 into Redshift nonstop.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: I thought that backfill was supposed to finish by Friday?

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: It was, but the job hit a bug where it retries on every transient network error, and those retries double the compute time. We're now at 42 hours of cluster uptime instead of the planned 8.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: So the extra cluster hours are what's inflating the bill?

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: Exactly. Each extra hour on the dc2.large nodes is $0.25, and we have eight of them, so those runaway hours added roughly $9,600 alone.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Do we have a kill switch? Can we pause it and investigate?

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: We can abort it, but we'd lose the progress and have to start over, which would push the timeline for the feature rollout.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: Maybe we can checkpoint the work, move the completed partitions to a temp table, and then restart a smaller backfill?

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: That's a possibility, but we'd need to re‑architect the job quickly, and the ops team is already stretched with the migration window prep.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: If we don't stop it now, the cost keeps climbing. We need a decision.

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: I'm leaning toward pausing it this afternoon, analyzing the retry loop, and then restarting with a throttling flag so we don't hammer the network.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Just a quick update on the cohort builder: the latest profiling run shows the latency dropped from 3.7 seconds to 2.1 seconds per request after we indexed the user_events view.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: That's solid progress, Rachel. Anything else?

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Yeah, the real win came after we applied the Fielder complaint fix—remember the ticket where Fielder said the UI was freezing on cohorts larger than 100k?

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: We moved the aggregation from the application layer into the new query engine rewrite, pushed the heavy lifting to the database, and added a materialized summary table that refreshes nightly.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Did that also cut the memory footprint?

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Exactly. Memory usage on the frontend dropped from roughly 850 MB to under 300 MB, which means the Chrome tab no longer spikes and users can stay on the page without a reload.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: We ran a load test with 250k synthetic users; the response time stayed under 2.5 seconds, and the error rate was zero, which directly addresses the Fielder team's pain point about timeouts.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Great, can we roll that out to staging by tomorrow?

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: I’m pushing the changes to the staging branch now; should be live by EOD. I’ll ping the QA lead to start regression testing, and I’ll update the Fielder team so they can verify the fix on their side.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Alright, so the migration script for the events table—yeah, that's the blocker we need to iron out today.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Exactly, we can't push it without a maintenance window, and we haven't got one on the calendar yet.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: We could maybe do a rolling upgrade, but that would require a bunch of extra coordination with the ops team.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: I hear you, but let me take this on. I’ll reach out to support and the ops lead, see if we can carve out a two‑hour window early next week, maybe Wednesday at 02:00 UTC.

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: Make sure you get the DBA sign‑off, otherwise they'll push back on the lock timeout settings.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Will do. I’ll set up a quick Slack thread with the support engineers, pull the change‑request ticket #4529, and ask them to confirm the impact analysis by tomorrow afternoon.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Cool, once we have that window locked in we can freeze the backfill and resume it after the cutover without blowing up the cost.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Great, I’ll update the sprint board once I have confirmation, and I'll ping everyone here with the scheduled slot so we can adjust our testing timelines accordingly.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Before we wrap, just a heads‑up: the on‑call rotation is shifting next sprint, so the primary pager for backend incidents moves from Tom to Yuki on Monday.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: Got it, thanks. That means I’ll need the escalation contacts updated in the run‑book, and I should probably shadow a couple of Tom’s alerts this week to get up to speed.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: Yeah, I can pull the recent incident logs and walk you through the typical failure patterns, especially the ones around the events table migration retries.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Also, the rotation change means the frontend alerts will now go to Chris, right? I’ll make sure the alert routing in PagerDuty reflects that by end of day.

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: Exactly, I’ll take over the infra‑related alerts. I’ll update the on‑call schedule in the ops calendar and add a note about the new escalation path for database lock timeouts.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: One thing—if we’re moving the primary on‑call, can we also bump the secondary backup window from 30 minutes to an hour, just in case the handoff takes longer than usual during the migration?

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Good point, Yuki. I’ll adjust the secondary window to 60 minutes in the schedule, and I’ll send out a revised on‑call roster email after this call so everyone has the latest version.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Alright, that's everything for today—thanks everyone for the updates, and let's keep an eye on that maintenance window.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: Sounds good, I'll watch for the Slack thread and start prepping the run‑book changes.

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: I'll freeze the backfill as soon as we get the slot, and I'll sync with you, Yuki, on the retry logic.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: I'll double‑check the frontend alert routing and push the PagerDuty update before EOD.

turns.speaker: Chris Lindqvist
turns.text: I'll monitor the cost spike after the backfill resumes and let the team know if anything looks off.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Great. I'll get the DBA sign‑off today, push ticket #4529 through the change‑request pipeline, and send the revised on‑call roster by 3 pm. I'll also add a quick note to the sprint board linking the maintenance window ticket, so everyone can see the status at a glance. If anything changes before then, drop a note in the thread.

turns.speaker: Yuki Tanaka
turns.text: Will do. Also, just a heads‑up—I saw a minor glitch in the query planner test on branch feature/agg‑v2, but it's isolated.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Noted, Yuki. We'll add that to the sprint backlog and prioritize a fix after the migration. Anything else?

turns.speaker: Tom Bradley
turns.text: No, I'm good.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Okay, then meeting adjourned. See you all tomorrow at 9 am.
